video_title: Climbing the AI Bubble Wall of Worry
gist: Jordi Visser argues the AI bubble thesis is wrong because agent-driven demand for compute exceeds supply, and that the real bubble is rate-dependent legacy companies. He extends this to a coming disruption of banks via Stripe-style agentic commerce, tokenization and crypto/privacy, with 2027 as a compute, AI and crypto year.

insights.claim: Visser distinguishes speculative, capacity and credit bubbles and argues none applies to AI today: Nvidia trades at a mid-teens multiple rather than Cisco-style 100x, demand exceeds supply for compute, and AI debt is largely asset-backed against compute whose prices are rising.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bubble-call tests should be run on the three types; only a supply-ahead-of-demand signal would flip the view.
insights.quote: The question for AI is supply getting ahead of demand.

insights.claim: Past bubbles had humans on both demand and supply sides; this cycle's demand comes from AI agents (thousands now, billions next year, eventually trillions) working far more hours than humans, so a persistent supply deficit is likely and historical bubble analogies mislead.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Demand-side modelling built on human headcount understates compute need.
insights.quote: The demand side is coming from agents.

insights.claim: The real bubble is in old-economy companies kept alive by zero rates, not in the digital economy; that is why roughly 400 S&P stocks fall while 100 rise, and the correct framing is long AI, short anything that needs low rates.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Position as a long/short on rate-dependence rather than treating AI as the froth.
insights.quote: The short side is everything that needs rates to be at zero.

insights.claim: Dalio's warning that AI may burst is dismissed as perma-bear endgame bias; Visser notes the call coincided with rising bond-market stress and treats both as possible reversal signals for rate-sensitive assets rather than for AI.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Treat high-profile bubble warnings as sentiment contrarian signals.

insights.claim: S&P has repeatedly shrugged off shocks (COVID ~40% drawdown, ~30% in 2022, ~20% on tariffs, fastest rate hikes since the 1980s, record bank run, oil-to-$200 Hormuz fears), which Visser reads as evidence there is no bubble burst; 20-30% corrections are still expected to occur.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Dips are likely buyable within the exponential regime, but drawdown risk of 20-30% should be sized for.

insights.claim: Historical gaps between all-time highs were long after real bubbles (about 7 years after 1973, until the iPhone era after 2000, until 2013 after 2007), whereas 2022 took only about 500 days, so the post-iPhone regime shows corrections rather than bubble unwinds.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Recovery speed supports the 'innovation index' view of the S&P.

insights.claim: Agent demand for tokens will far exceed supply, and anticipated efficiency gains will not close the gap; Visser likens compute to oil, which scales with nominal GDP, while agents multiply faster than any human-driven driver.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity and data-center delays keep the infrastructure trade supported.
insights.quote: We don't have enough tokens for what's coming.

insights.claim: The agent trade should be expressed through compute suppliers, not by trying to pick the winning personal-agent platform; Meta, Amazon/Alexa, Apple/Siri and Google compete for the same TAM and it is unclear who monetizes.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Own the picks-and-shovels layer rather than the consumer-agent contest.

insights.claim: Alpha rotated in phases: first Nvidia and power (Vistra, turbines) for compute brains, then memory after Opus 4.5 in November, with Micron going from 100 to 200 over seven months and 200 to 400 over the next five; Visser says most investors missed the memory move and expects further 3-4x moves in certain components.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Look for the next bottleneck component in the agent stack.

insights.claim: Lumentum's CEO said the company is completely sold out through 2029, which Visser cites as refutation of the claim that AI demand is not there through that date.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Optical supply constraints are multi-year.
insights.quote: We are completely sold out through 2029.

insights.claim: Cloudflare had forecast AI bots overtaking web traffic by 2027, and the speaker cited by Visser has since said it has already happened.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Agent traffic is arriving earlier than planned.

insights.claim: Visser dismisses bearish revenue-requirement math on AI capex as linear thinking relying on a six-month-old paper from before personal agents and coding agents had adoption.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Capex-vs-revenue bear models are stale in an exponential adoption curve.

insights.claim: Visser holds a personal estimate of about $70 billion annualized revenue for OpenAI by year-end and dismisses recent negative OpenAI headlines as noise.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A benchmark to judge OpenAI-related negative news against.

insights.claim: Narrow breadth is a symptom of rate-sensitive old-economy weakness, not market fragility: utilities 18%, staples 33%, durables 30% and autos 12% of stocks sit above their 200-day, versus technology 73% and financials 74%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Weak breadth is not a top signal while tech and hyperscalers hold.

insights.claim: Since ChatGPT's launch, only semis/tech, energy and capital goods have meaningfully beaten the index, and only 24% of S&P 1500 names outperformed versus 71% of Visser's 59-stock agentic basket in the S&P 1500; dispersion makes name-by-name or 40-act style management hard.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Concentration is required; diversified portfolios are structurally fighting the tape.

insights.claim: An equal-weight S&P MACD buy signal fired this week; since 2007 it has reportedly been right 22 out of 22 times at 6 months, with 91% at 3 months and 90% at 12 months, and Visser reads oversold breadth as a bounce setup in zombie companies as hedge funds cover shorts.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Tactical bounce in laggards is likely, not a regime change.

insights.claim: Europe, small caps (IWM versus QQQ) and the 'broadening out' trade underperform because they are the reverse of the exponential-innovation trade; the US is 56% technology.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Broadening-out and international overweights have been structurally losing bets.

insights.claim: Watch-list indicators: Morgan Stanley leverage factor falling while the S&P is at highs, triple-C spreads widening against stable triple-Bs (weak credit being cleared out), and hyperscaler weakness, which Visser says would be the true worry signal.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Stress in weak credit is benign unless it spreads to hyperscalers.

insights.claim: The 10-year yield shows triple RSI divergence against price while the MOVE index had an outside reversal week, suggesting rate pressure is tiring; flat yields over a year would not be bearish for stocks.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bond reversal may relieve rate-sensitive sectors.

insights.claim: Henry McVey (KKR) now sees a broader, more durable and more inflationary global investment cycle (defense, infrastructure, Europe and Asia strong) with corporate profits rising rapidly while labor is not; earnings can outrun higher rates given nominal GDP growth.
insights.speaker: Henry McVey (cited by Visser)
insights.so_what: Profit-versus-labor divergence is a 2027 theme.

insights.claim: Labor weakness is the likely next pressure point on bonds: healthcare openings and hiring have slowed over six months, jobs 'plentiful vs hard to get' is deteriorating, and negative payroll prints could become regular if healthcare stops supporting the total.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Rising agent adoption worsens the labor-versus-capital gap.

insights.claim: 2027 could be the first year agents' productive work exceeds that of roughly 4-5 billion people and feel like a century of progress; Visser expects chaos but not a reason to be bearish on earnings.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Position for an acceleration year in compute, AI and crypto.
insights.quote: 2027 could feel like 100 years worth of progress compressed into a single year.

insights.claim: Banks face a 'bank apocalypse' analogous to the SaaS selloff within roughly nine months as consumer agents arrive; Visser is not forecasting collapse or advocating shorts, only that a flinch in revenue could trigger a repricing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Banks sit in the 'disrupted' bucket alongside SaaS rather than adapters.

insights.claim: Stripe is cited as the template for the AI-native financial stack: H1 net revenue +41%, billing +71%, free cash flow +43%, over 100,000 Stripe Capital loans, acquisitions of Privy, Bridge, Metronome and OpenRouter, versus Citigroup's 226,000 employees and Stripe's 10,000 with a $160-214B valuation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fast-growing infrastructure firms take share from slow banks.

insights.claim: Agents plus legacy rails (SWIFT, multi-day wires) are unworkable; Visser notes a bank wire to Robinhood took 5 days while Robinhood to Coinbase took 5 seconds, and expects instant settlement, metered micro-billing and tokenized rails to win.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Supports stablecoin and crypto settlement over card networks for agent payments.

insights.claim: Tokenization and 24/7 trading (168 hours vs about 32.5 hours of equity trading) is bad for market-neutral funds and options traders, raises LTCM-style leverage risk, and requires repricing options and liquidity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Multi-strat leverage structures are vulnerable to continuous trading.

insights.claim: Buckets for stocks: adapters, winners (semis) and the disrupted (SaaS); disruption means massive drawdowns, so portfolio managers must be concentrated rather than diversified.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Classify holdings by AI exposure rather than sector.

insights.claim: Visser expects the biggest crypto gains because institutions are not yet positioned: hedge and mutual funds have already priced compute but won't buy crypto until forced; crypto upside requires fundamentals plus inflows from other investors.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Crypto is the under-owned leg of the agentic trade for 2027.

insights.claim: Agentic AI turns privacy into a control problem, so Visser wants to be long a privacy theme (Zcash, NEAR and others), drawing on Vitalik Buterin's argument that AI reconstructs behavior from data.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Privacy tokens are a second-order agent beneficiary.

insights.claim: Visser sees stablecoin and tokenization momentum in Asia and institutions (Samsung adding USDC to its wallet, Standard Chartered custody in Singapore, OKX filing for tokenized stock trading, IMF acknowledging tokenized assets) as supporting his agent-crypto link.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Incumbent adoption is building.
